Pelagius II
pə-lā'jē-əs
n. (Pelagius II, bishop of Rome 579–590, who objected to the title of ecumenical patriarch and sent Gregory to Constantinople)
Greek pelagios, of the sea, from pelagos, the open sea; unrelated to the British heretic of the same name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Pelagius II was elected in 579 while the Lombards were besieging Rome, and his pontificate was spent on two fronts. The first was survival: he sought help from Constantinople and, failing to get it, bought the Lombards off and turned to the Franks. He sent the deacon Gregory, afterwards Gregory the Great, as his representative to the imperial court, where Gregory spent six formative years. The second front was a title. When John IV of Constantinople, called the Faster, took or accepted the style of ecumenical patriarch, Pelagius objected and declared the acts of a synod held under it void — the beginning of the dispute Gregory would continue, calling the title a mark of the forerunner of antichrist. Mat 20:25 is the text the objection rested on, that dominion so exercised is the way of “the princes of the Gentiles” (Mat 20:25).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines ecumenical as general, universal, and preeminence as superiority, the state of being the chief.

expand to see more

ECUMEN'ICAL, a. General; universal; as an ecumenical council.

PREEM'INENCE, n. Superiority in degree; precedence; the state of being the chief or principal.

TI'TLE, n. An appellation of dignity, distinction or preeminence given to persons.

Key Scripture

Mat 20:25 — "But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them."

Mat 20:26 — "But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;"

3Jn 1:9 — "I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not."

Mat 23:9 — "And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven."

Modern Corruption

A bishop of Rome denounced the title of universal patriarch, and his successors took one just like it.

expand to see more

The irony here is the dictionary's whole point about the papal office, and it is not a cheap one. Pelagius II, and Gregory the Great after him, were right: a title claiming universal jurisdiction over the churches is contrary to Christ's express order for His ministers. Mat 20:26 states it as plainly as anything in the New Testament, that “it shall not be so among you” (Mat 20:26), and 3Jn 1:9 names the fault in a particular man, Diotrephes, “who loveth to have the preeminence among them” (3Jn 1:9).

Within two centuries the Roman see was claiming, by a more sweeping right than John the Faster had ever asserted, exactly what Pelagius had declared void in another. The dictionary holds that the argument of 579 was sound and that the Roman see is the chief defendant under it. Mat 23:9 forbids the title of father on earth; the papal office is built on both the title and the universal jurisdiction. The Lombard crisis is worth remembering alongside it: Pelagius died of plague in 590 with the city starving, and the man he had trained in Constantinople inherited all of it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek katakurieuo (G2634), to lord over; diakonos (G1249), a servant; philoproteuo (G5383), to love preeminence.

Greek katakurieuo (G2634) — to exercise dominion over; Matthew 20:25.

Greek katexousiazo (G2715) — to exercise authority upon; Matthew 20:25.

Usage

"“the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them” (Mat 20:25) — the objection's ground."

"“it shall not be so among you” (Mat 20:26) — stated as plainly as anything."

"“who loveth to have the preeminence among them” (3Jn 1:9) — named in a man."
